A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Florida Everglade's macroinvertebrate and fish community is highly sensitive to changes in hydrology, nutrients and predation.

nutrient enrichment of the Everglades ecosystem has increased the amount of periphyton available to support macroinvertebrates, small fish and other consumers, but has also increased the amount of algae available to consumers that are not infaunal.

we quantified the effects of nutrient enrichment (bottom-up) and hydrological disturbance (bottom-up and top-down) on periphyton community structure and biomass and the indirect effects of these factors on macroinvertebrate and small fish densities.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the indirect effects of nutrients, hydrological disturbance and predation can be quantified in wetlands and can be important in structuring wetland communities, even when direct effects of these factors are small or non-existent.
the Everglades ecosystem is highly complex and that there are multiple mechanisms that can influence the abundance of different groups of organisms.
nutrient levels and disturbance have both direct and indirect effects on consumers in the Everglades, and that the relative importance of these factors is dependent on consumer type.
